title: Without Clear Shape
core: All four describe something you can't get a firm outline around — no edges, no fixed limit, no centre of gravity. The confusion is that each locates the shapelessness somewhere different: in the object itself, in how early it is, in a limit nobody set, or in how thinly the material is spread. Only one of them implies the thing is too *new* to have form; only one implies there's plenty of substance, just no focus. Get the source of the formlessness right and the four stop overlapping.

words.nuance: The purely spatial one: **amorphous** says the thing has no outline, full stop — no claim about when it started, who blurred it, or whether it will ever firm up. It's the only member with a real technical sense (glass, non-crystalline solids), which is why even its critical use sounds like a diagnosis rather than a complaint.

The only one that timestamps the shapelessness: **inchoate** things are formless *because they have barely begun*. It attaches naturally to feelings and movements too new to be named — inchoate rage, an inchoate movement — where amorphous would suggest the thing has simply always been a blob.

The only one about a limit that was never *set*, usually by somebody who could have set it. **Indefinite** covers duration as readily as outline — indefinite leave, detained indefinitely — and its chill comes from a withheld commitment, not from any lack of form in the thing itself.

The only one where the substance is all present and merely spread too thin to land: a **diffuse** essay has plenty of content, just no centre. It's also the only verb here (heat, light, power diffuse outward), and as a criticism it opposes *concise* and *trenchant*, not *defined*.

exam_note: Traps swap **inchoate** for "incomplete" (it means barely begun, not half-finished) and **diffuse** for "vague" or "empty" (the material is there — it just never concentrates).
